tile: Every document in your casefile, with a walk-through beside it. It won't answer for you. It shows you how.

walk.say: Before you read a word of the document, read the line above it. Who made it, when, and why?

walk.step: Read it once, all the way.
walk.say: Start to finish, no stopping. Hit a hard word? Keep going. Then say what it's about in a few words.
walk.say_image: Look in three passes: the title and labels, then the biggest thing, then the small details.

casefiles.title: 11.1 Casefile A · Contact, Consequence, and the Colonial Economies

docs.title: The Town of Secota
docs.src: Source: Theodor de Bry, engraver, 1590 (adapted). De Bry worked in Frankfurt from watercolors painted in Virginia by John White. De Bry never crossed the Atlantic.

steps.question: Who made this picture, where, and for whom?
steps.line: Read the whole source line. Count the hands between Secota and you: who painted it, who carved it, and who bought it.
Use the page's Five Looks: frame, people, words, what is centered, what is missing. One pass for each.

steps.question: What does this picture show about life in Secota? Find three details that prove it.
steps.line: Split the picture into four corners and the center street. Look for people doing something in each part, and look at the fields.

steps.question: Whose view is this, and whose voice is missing?
steps.line: The people of Secota didn't make this picture. Ask what a buyer in Europe in 1590 hoped to see.

steps.question: If the land was already full of towns and farms, what does that say about who had a right to it?
steps.line: Put the picture next to the word settlement. What does that word assume about the land?

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 1's questions in your casefile, starting on page 5. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

docs.title: An English traveler counts the dead
docs.src: Source: John Josselyn, An Account of Two Voyages to New-England, Made during the Years 1638, 1663

steps.question: Who wrote this, and did he see all of it himself?
steps.line: Check the dates in the source line, then the first words of the passage. When did these deaths happen, and when did he arrive?
It was written more than 300 years ago, so read it once for the story, then once more slowly. Mortality and sagamorship are in your word list on page 4.

steps.question: What does Josselyn say happened to Native peoples, and what numbers back it up?
steps.line: Find the word "first" and the word "afterwards." Then look for the word "from."

steps.question: Whose view is this, and whose voices are missing?
steps.line: Notice whose numbers he gives. Is any Native person quoted?

steps.question: If disease emptied the land, did that make the land free to take? Who gets to decide?
steps.line: Ask who is doing the claiming, and who isn't there to say no.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 2's questions in your casefile, starting on page 6. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: ….Not long before the English came into the Country, happened a great mortality amongst [Native Americans], especially where the English afterwards planted, the East and Northern parts were sore smitten with the Contagion; first by the plague, afterwards when the English came by the small pox, the three Kingdoms or Sagamorships of the Massachusetts were very populous, having under them seven Dukedoms or petti-Sagamorships, but by the plague were brought from 30,000 to 300. There are not many now to the Eastward, the Pequots were destroyed by the English: the Mohawks are about five hundred….

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Not long before the English came into the Country, a great mortality (many deaths) happened among [Native Americans]. It struck especially where the English afterwards planted (settled). The East and Northern parts were hit hard by the Contagion (a disease that spreads). It came first by the plague, and afterwards, when the English came, by the small pox. The three Kingdoms or Sagamorships (lands ruled by Native leaders) of the Massachusetts once had many people, with seven smaller Sagamorships under them. But by the plague they were brought from 30,000 to 300. There are not many left now to the East. The Pequots were destroyed by the English. The Mohawks are about five hundred.

docs.title: The same story in numbers
docs.src: Source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History (adapted)

steps.question: Who made these tables, and how exact are the numbers?
steps.line: Read the source line and the title. One word in the title tells you how sure these numbers are.
Title first. Then the top table, one row at a time, then the bottom table. "c." before a year means about, and "100s" means a few hundred.

steps.question: What do the two tables show when you read them together?
steps.line: Read the first row of each table across. Which way is each number moving?

steps.question: Whose numbers are probably the roughest guess, and why?
steps.line: Ask who was keeping records in 1610, and whose numbers they cared about.

steps.question: When a population drops this far, who, if anyone, is responsible?
steps.line: First list the causes you've seen in Documents 2 and 3. Then ask which of them a person could answer for.

docs.title: A warning
docs.src: Source: Miantonomo, Narragansett sachem, speaking to the Montaukett on Long Island, c. 1642. Recorded by an English listener and printed later in Great Native American Speeches.

steps.question: Who spoke these words, who wrote them down, and why does that matter?
steps.line: Read the source line all the way to the end. He spoke; someone else wrote. What could change between the two?
Two paragraphs: the first is how things were, and the second is what changed. Words in [brackets] were added to help you.

steps.question: What is Miantonomo asking his listeners to do, and what reasons does he give?
steps.line: His first sentence is the ask. The reasons are the before and after: what their fathers had, and what the English changed.

steps.question: Whose view is this? How would an English colonist tell the same story?
steps.line: Look at the word he uses for what the English did to the country. Would a colonist use that word?

steps.question: Why would joining together matter to peoples who are losing their land?
steps.line: Find his first sentence and hold on to it. The same idea comes back in Casefile B.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 4's questions in your casefile, starting on page 8. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: Brothers, we must be as one as the English are, or we shall all be destroyed. You know our fathers had plenty of deer and skins and our plains were full of game and turkeys, and our coves and rivers were full of fish.

But, brothers, since these Englishmen have seized our country, they have cut down the grass with scythes, and the trees with axes. Their cows and horses eat up the grass, and their hogs spoil our bed of clams; and finally we shall all starve to death; therefore, stand not in your own light, I ask you, but resolve to act like men. All the sachems [tribal chiefs] both to the east and the west have joined with us, and we are resolved to fall upon them at a day appointed, and therefore I come secretly to you, cause you can persuade your Indians [Native Americans] to do what you will.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Brothers, we must be as one, the way the English are, or we shall all be destroyed. You know our fathers had plenty of deer and skins. Our plains were full of game and turkeys, and our coves and rivers were full of fish.

But, brothers, these Englishmen have seized (taken) our country. They have cut down the grass with scythes and the trees with axes. Their cows and horses eat up the grass, and their hogs spoil our bed of clams. In the end we shall all starve to death. So do not stand in your own way, I ask you. Make up your minds to act like men. All the sachems [tribal chiefs] to the east and the west have joined with us. We have decided to attack them on a day we choose. That is why I come to you in secret, because you can persuade your Indians [Native Americans] to do what you want.

licence.text: As printed on the NYSED Regents exam in US History and Government, January 2024.

docs.title: A treaty, and what was said at it
docs.src: Source: The Lancaster Treaty of 1744. The speaker, Gachradodow, was an Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) orator addressing colonial negotiators from Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania.

steps.question: Who is speaking, to whom, and who wrote it down?
steps.line: The source line names the speaker and his listeners. The line just before the speech is someone else describing him.
The bold line at the top is a quote from the speech. Assaragoa is the name the Iroquois used for Virginia's governor. Read it like a speech said out loud.

steps.question: What does Gachradodow claim about the two peoples, and how does he back it up?
steps.line: Start with the bold line at the top. Then find the word "placed" and his last sentence about land.

steps.question: Whose view is this, and how might the colonial negotiators answer him?
steps.line: Picture the men from Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania across the table. What did they come to this meeting for?

steps.question: What right is Gachradodow defending for his people?
steps.line: Reread the bold line at the top. It's about who has the right to make the laws on this land. The Native American arc of Thread 1 asks about it by name.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 5's questions in your casefile, starting on page 9. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “You have your Laws and Customs, so have we.”
—Gachradodow
Pennsylvania, 1744
. . . Gachradodow in a strong voice, and with a proper action, spoke as follows:

“Great Assaragoa, The World at the first was made on the other Side of the Great Water, different from what it is on this Side, as may be known from the different Colors of our Skin and of our Flesh, and that which you call Justice may not be so amongst us. You have your Laws and Customs, and so have we. The Great King might send you over to conquer the Indians [Native Americans], but it looks to us that God did not approve of it. If he had, he would not have placed the Sea where it is, as the Limits between us and you. . . .

Brother Assaragoa . . . You know very well when the white people came first here, they were poor; but now they have got lands and are by them become rich, and we are now poor: what little we have had for the land goes soon away, but the land lasts forever.” . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “You have your Laws and Customs, so have we.”
—Gachradodow
Pennsylvania, 1744
Gachradodow spoke in a strong voice, with the right gestures. He said:

“Great Assaragoa, the World was first made on the other Side of the Great Water, different from how it is on this Side. You can tell from the different Colors of our Skin and of our Flesh. What you call Justice may not be justice to us. You have your Laws and Customs, and so have we. The Great King might send you over to conquer the Indians [Native Americans]. But it looks to us that God did not approve of it. If he had, he would not have placed the Sea where it is, as the Limits (border) between us and you.

Brother Assaragoa, you know very well that when the white people first came here, they were poor. But now they have got lands, and the lands have made them rich. And we are now poor. What little we got for the land is soon gone, but the land lasts forever.”

licence.text: As printed on the NYSED Regents exam in US History and Government, June 2026.

docs.title: The trade
docs.src: Source: The Making of America, National Geographic Society (adapted)

steps.question: Who made this map, and when, compared with the trade it shows?
steps.line: The source line names a modern publisher. Ask how a mapmaker today knows what was shipped centuries ago.
Do what the page says: read the key first, then the arrows. Trace each arrow from its tail to its head.

steps.question: What does the map show about how the colonies made money?
steps.line: Read the key first. Then follow the solid arrows leaving the colonies and read the words along them.

steps.question: On two arrows, people are listed with sugar and gold. Whose point of view does that show, and who is left out?
steps.line: Ask who did the buying and selling, and who was carried. Which of them would list it this way?

steps.question: If a country's wealth is built on a route like this one, what is that country responsible for?
steps.line: Take a side, then give one reason from the map. There's no single right answer here, only one you can back up.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 6's questions in your casefile, starting on page 10. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

casefiles.title: 11.1 Casefile B · Who Paid for It

docs.title: Two kinds of bound labor
docs.src: Source: adapted from New Visions for Public Schools, US.01.C.2.

steps.question: Who made this chart, and when? Is it from the colonial era?
steps.line: Read the source line. Teachers made this chart recently, from older records. Ask what a chart like this can show, and what it can't.
It's a chart set as text: two columns, each with Who, Work and Terms. Read all of one column, then all of the other, then compare them row by row.

steps.question: What is the biggest difference between the two columns?
steps.line: Read the Terms row in both columns. Find the line in one column that the other can't match at any price.

steps.question: Who chose which facts go side by side? What might the columns leave out?
steps.line: Two columns make things look neat and even. Ask whose experience a neat row of facts can't hold.

steps.question: Why is the difference between these columns a question about law, not just about work?
steps.line: Look at what happens to children in each column, and what the law allowed. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 8's questions in your casefile, starting on page 4. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: INDENTURED SERVANTS (1607 – early 1700s)
Who: Chose to immigrate from Europe under contract. Mostly the poorest class, or criminals, looking for a fresh start.
Work: Hard labor — clearing land, building farms and towns; field work; skilled trades: bricklaying, building, sewing, cooking.
Terms: Contract of 3–7 years, usually one master. In exchange: passage, room, lodging, food. Freedom dues at the end — land, clothes, a year's corn. Some legal protections.
ENSLAVED PEOPLE (1619–1776)
Who: Native people captured in America; African people forced to immigrate against their will — kidnapped or sold in Africa, then carried here.
Work: Hard labor; farm hands, often on large plantations; some worked in houses — sewing, cooking, cleaning.

Terms: Little pay for mostly lifelong service. Could sometimes earn or buy freedom. Children of enslaved people were also enslaved. Could be bought and sold. Little to no protection against abuse. Could legally be killed.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: INDENTURED SERVANTS (1607 to the early 1700s)
Who: People from Europe who chose to come here under a contract. Most were very poor, and some were criminals. They wanted a fresh start.
Work: Hard labor, like clearing land and building farms and towns. Field work. Skilled jobs like bricklaying, building, sewing and cooking.

Terms: A contract (a written deal) for 3 to 7 years, usually with one master. In return they got the trip over, a place to live, and food. At the end they got freedom dues: land, clothes, and a year's corn. The law gave them some protection.
ENSLAVED PEOPLE (1619 to 1776)
Who: Native people captured in America, and African people forced to come here against their will. They were kidnapped or sold in Africa, then carried here.
Work: Hard labor. Farm work, often on large plantations. Some worked in houses, sewing, cooking and cleaning.

Terms: Little pay, for service that mostly lasted their whole lives. Sometimes they could earn or buy their freedom. Their children were enslaved too. They could be bought and sold. The law gave them little or no protection from abuse. They could legally be killed.

docs.title: The contract
docs.src: Source: Virtual Jamestown. Indenture of Richard Lowther, 1627.

steps.question: Who made this agreement, and did Lowther choose to sign it?
steps.line: Read the first lines: two men are named. Lowther signed this himself. Ask what he expected to get out of it.
Old legal English, with … where words were cut. Read it once for who promises what. Heirs are the people who inherit from you.

steps.question: What does each side promise the other?
steps.line: Find the four years and what Lowther owes. Then find what Hurd promises, during the term and at the end.

steps.question: Is this a fair deal? Whose side of it are we not hearing?
steps.line: Hurd's side is written in. Picture Lowther four years later in Virginia. What could go wrong that the contract doesn't mention?

steps.question: What does a contract protect, and who does it protect most?
steps.line: Ask who wrote the terms, and who had to accept them. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 9's questions in your casefile, starting on page 6. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: This writing… between Richard Lowther of Broom in Southill in the County of Bedford, and Edward Hurd citizen and iron monger of London… said Richard Lowther has presently pledges a covenant to agree and bind himself to be a servant of him the said Edward Hurd and heirs who assign him to be sent and transported unto the country and land of Virginia… and to be employed by Hurd and heirs upon his plantation there, and for during the space of four years… during which said term the said Richard Lowther shall and will truly employ and endeavor himself to the utmost power of his knowledge and skill to perform true and faithful service…

Edward Hurd and heirs do promise and grant to Richard Lowther transport to Virginia and find and provide him sufficient meat and drink clothing and any other necessaries for his livelihood and maintenance during the said term but also at the expiration of the said term shall and will grant the said Richard Lowther the quantity of 50 acres of land in Virginia to him…
[made the last day of July 1627, in the third year of the reign of King Charles]

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: This contract is between Richard Lowther, of Broom in the County of Bedford, and Edward Hurd, an iron merchant of London. Richard Lowther agrees to bind himself as a servant to Edward Hurd and his heirs. He will be sent to Virginia and work on Hurd's plantation there for four years. During that time Lowther will work as hard and as well as he can, and give true and faithful service.

In return, Edward Hurd and his heirs promise to carry Lowther to Virginia. During the four years they will give him enough food, drink, clothing and everything else he needs to live. When the four years are over, they will give Richard Lowther 50 acres of land in Virginia.
[made the last day of July 1627, in the third year of the reign of King Charles]

docs.title: The letter home
docs.src: Source: Virtual Jamestown. Richard Frethorne to his parents, 1623.

steps.question: Who wrote this, to whom, and what does he want from them?
steps.line: Frethorne is sixteen, and he's writing to the people who could send help. Read the last paragraph first, then start at the top.
Four parts: the greeting, then sickness and food, then fear and clothes, then his request. Gruel is a thin, watery porridge.

steps.question: What is life like for Frethorne in Virginia? Name two conditions.
steps.line: Look for food, sickness, clothes and fear. Each paragraph gives you at least one.

steps.question: How might his reason for writing shape what he tells his parents?
steps.line: Ask what a boy who wants to be bought out needs his parents to believe. Then ask what he might leave out.

steps.question: He came under a contract like Lowther's. Who was the law really protecting?
steps.line: Put Document 9's promises next to this letter. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 10's questions in your casefile, starting on page 8. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: Loving and kind father and mother,

…This is to let you understand that I your child (though at 16 years hardly a child) am in a most heavy case by reason of the country, [which] is such that it causes much sickness, such as the scurvy and the dysentery and diverse other diseases… And when we are sick there is nothing to comfort us; for since I came out of the ship I never ate anything but peas, and loblollie (that is, water gruel)… we must work hard both early and late for a mess of water gruel and a mouthful of bread and beef…

For we live in fear of the enemy Natives every hour… we are but 32 to fight against 3000 Natives if they should come… And I have nothing to comfort me… not a shirt to my back but two rags, nor clothes but one poor suit, nor but one pair of shoes, but one pair of stockings, but one cap…

Goodman Jackson… much marveled that you would send me a servant to the Company; he said I had been better off if I had knocked on the head. And indeed so I find it now, to my great grief and misery; and I say that if you love me you will redeem me suddenly, for which I do entreat and beg…

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Loving and kind father and mother,

I want you to understand that I, your child (though at 16 years old I am hardly a child), am in a very hard place because of this country. It causes a lot of sickness, like scurvy and dysentery and other diseases. When we are sick there is nothing to comfort us. Since I got off the ship I have eaten nothing but peas and loblollie (that is, water gruel, a thin porridge). We must work hard, early and late, for a bowl of water gruel and a mouthful of bread and beef.

We live in fear of the enemy Natives every hour. There are only 32 of us to fight against 3000 Natives if they come. I have nothing to comfort me. I have no shirt on my back but two rags, only one poor suit of clothes, one pair of shoes, one pair of stockings, one cap.

Goodman Jackson was amazed that you would send me here as a servant to the Company. He said I had been better off if I had knocked on the head (been killed). And now I find that is true, to my great grief and misery. I say that if you love me you will redeem me (buy me out) suddenly. I beg you to.

docs.title: Two notices
docs.src: A — Source: Higher Education and Slavery in Western Massachusetts. B — Source: New York Public Library Manuscript Collection.

steps.question: What kind of document is each one, and what job was it written to do?
steps.line: Read the label above each one. Neither was written to describe slavery. Each was written to get something done.
Two short documents. Read A, then B. In B, read the whole list without stopping, all the way to the end.

steps.question: What do these two notices show about how enslaved people were treated under the law?
steps.line: In A, find Prince's age and how long he is sold for. In B, read the list in order: what comes right after the people?

steps.question: Whose voice is missing from both notices?
steps.line: Count the people named or listed. Now count how many of them say a word.

steps.question: What principle had to be missing for a nine-year-old to be sold in an ordinary contract?
steps.line: Look in the group called What government must protect. Read each name and ask which ones Prince was denied.

text: A · BILL OF SALE, 1750

For and in consideration of the sum of two hundred and twenty five pounds… to me Ephraim Williams Jr. well and truly paid by Israel Williams of Hatfield, I do hereby assign, sell and convey to him a certain negro boy named Prince aged about nine years, a servant for life, and do hold him and his heirs against the claims of any person whatsoever as witness my hand this 25th day of September 1750.
B · AUCTION ANNOUNCEMENT, ESTATE OF ADOLPH PHILIPSE

To be sold at public auction… on the Manor of Philipsburg; Four Negro Men, namely a mill worker, a Boat-Man, and two farmers; three Negro women; namely two farm workers and one cook, six Negro boys, and two girls, household goods, and all the stock, consisting of 40 odd head of cattle, 26 horses, a number of sheep and hogs, and all the utensils belonging to the said manor.

text: A · BILL OF SALE, 1750

Israel Williams of Hatfield has paid me, Ephraim Williams Jr., two hundred and twenty five pounds. In return I sell and hand over to him a Black boy named Prince, aged about nine years, a servant for life. I promise that no one else has any claim to him. Signed by me on the 25th day of September 1750.

docs.title: A life, told by the person who lived it
docs.src: Source: Documenting the American South. Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture Smith, a Native of Africa, but resident above sixty years in the United States, related by himself.

steps.question: Who is telling this story, and when did he tell it?
steps.line: Read the whole source line: related by himself, after more than sixty years in this country. He's looking back on his whole life.
Four parts, with … where pages were skipped. Each part jumps ahead in his life: the sale, the work, the punishment, the family.

steps.question: What does Venture Smith's story show about how enslaved people were treated?
steps.line: Find what he was bought for, what he had to do at nine, and what happened to his family. Each paragraph adds one more.

steps.question: What can his own story tell you that an owner's paperwork never could?
steps.line: Put his story next to Document 11. Who is talking in each? What does only Venture know?

steps.question: Venture Smith bought his own freedom. Does that make the system fair?
steps.line: Ask what he had to do to buy it, and what he had already lost. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 12's questions in your casefile, starting on page 12. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: …It was 1738…. I was kidnapped in Africa…. our master told us all to appear to the best possible advantage for sale. I was brought on board by one Robertson Mumford, for four gallons of rum, and a piece of calico, and called VENTURE, on account of his having purchased me with his own private venture.

The first of the time of living at my master's own place, I was pretty much employed in the house at cleaning and picking wool… after which my master put me to work out of doors… to pound four bushels of ears of corn every night in a barrel for the poultry, or be rigorously punished… These tasks I had to perform when I was about nine years old.

…he then broke out into a great rage, snatched a pitchfork and went to lay me over the head therewith; but I as soon got another and defended myself… He took me to a gallows made for the purpose of hanging cattle on, and suspended me on it… I was released and went to work after hanging on the gallows about an hour.

…At the close of that year I was sold to a Thomas Stanton, and had to be separated from my wife and one daughter, who was about one month old… This money I got by cleaning gentlemen's shoes and drawing boots, by catching musk-rats and minks, raising potatoes and carrots, and by fishing in the night, and at odd spells.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: It was 1738. I was kidnapped in Africa. Our master told us all to look our best to be sold. I was brought on board a ship by Robertson Mumford, for four gallons of rum, and a piece of calico (cotton cloth). He called me VENTURE, because he bought me with his own private venture (his own money, as an investment).

When I first lived at my master's own place, I worked mostly in the house, cleaning and picking wool. After that my master put me to work outdoors. Every night I had to pound four bushels of ears of corn in a barrel for the chickens, or be harshly punished. These tasks I had to perform when I was about nine years old.

Then he flew into a great rage. He grabbed a pitchfork and went to hit me over the head with it, but I quickly got another one and defended myself. He took me to a gallows made for hanging cattle and hung me on it. I was let down and went back to work after hanging on the gallows about an hour.

At the end of that year I was sold to a Thomas Stanton, and had to be separated from my wife and one daughter, who was about one month old. I got this money by cleaning gentlemen's shoes and pulling off their boots, by catching muskrats and minks, raising potatoes and carrots, and by fishing at night and in my spare time.

docs.title: How a law gets built
docs.src: Compiled by New Visions for Public Schools from Ferris State University, PBS Slavery in America, and Colonial Williamsburg.

steps.question: Who made this timeline, and from what kinds of sources?
steps.line: Read the source line. Then notice what almost every entry is: a law, a court ruling, or what lawmakers did after an event.
Nothing here happened all at once. Read the years in order, top to bottom, and watch one step build on the last.

steps.question: What changes for Black people in the colonies between 1619 and 1705?
steps.line: Compare the first entry with the last. What were the twenty Africans called in 1619, and what does the law call enslaved people in 1705?

steps.question: Who wrote these laws, and whose voice is missing?
steps.line: Every line was written by the people making the law. Ask what this timeline would say if the people it was made about had kept it.

steps.question: Freedoms are taken away one law at a time. What principle is being broken?
steps.line: Look at 1640: the same offense, two different sentences. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 13's questions in your casefile, starting on page 18. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: 1619 · Jamestown: twenty captive Africans are sold and classified as indentured servants.
1640 · Three runaway servants are captured. The General Court gives the two white servants additional years to serve — and sentences John Punch, a Black man, to servitude for life.
1641 · Massachusetts becomes the first colony to legalize slavery.
1662 · Virginia decides any child born to an enslaved woman is also enslaved.
1664 · Maryland mandates lifelong servitude for all enslaved Black people. New York, New Jersey, the Carolinas and Virginia pass similar laws.
1669 · Virginia: an act on the “casual killing” of enslaved people — if a person dies resisting his master, it is not presumed to have been done with malice.
1676 · Bacon's Rebellion. Poor whites and Black servants fight side by side. The government's response hastens the shift to Black slavery and away from indentured servitude.
1694 · Rice cultivation begins in the Carolinas. Demand for enslaved labor rises sharply.

1705 · Virginia slave codes: all Black, mulatto and Indian enslaved people are declared real property — legally real estate. Forbidden to assault a white person, denied the right to bear arms, denied movement without written permission.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: 1619 · Jamestown: twenty Africans who had been captured are sold. They are called indentured servants.
1640 · Three servants run away and are caught. The court gives the two white servants more years to serve. It sentences John Punch, a Black man, to serve for life.
1641 · Massachusetts becomes the first colony to make slavery legal.
1662 · Virginia decides that any child born to an enslaved woman is also enslaved.
1664 · Maryland requires lifelong servitude for all enslaved Black people. New York, New Jersey, the Carolinas and Virginia pass similar laws.
1669 · Virginia passes a law about the “casual killing” of enslaved people. If an enslaved person dies while resisting his master, the law does not assume the master meant to kill.
1676 · Bacon's Rebellion. Poor white people and Black servants fight side by side. The government's response speeds up the shift to Black slavery and away from indentured servitude.
1694 · Rice farming begins in the Carolinas. The demand for enslaved workers rises sharply.

1705 · Virginia slave codes: all Black, mulatto (mixed-race) and Indian enslaved people are declared real property, which means legally real estate. They are forbidden to hit a white person, denied the right to carry weapons, and not allowed to travel without written permission.

steps.line: The writer's name is near the end. Ask who read the Virginia Gazette in 1751, and what Stith wanted them to do.
One long notice. Read it in pieces: what Tom looks like, what happened before, the reward, and the last line.

steps.question: What does this notice show about Tom?
steps.line: Find how many times he was caught, and what was done to him the last time. Then read the last line.

steps.question: Stith describes Tom to catch him. What does his description prove about Tom that Stith didn't mean to show?
steps.line: Ask what a man who keeps escaping, even in chains, is telling you about himself.

steps.question: What does the iron collar tell you about calling this system lawful?
steps.line: Look at the shackles and the collar. Then read your card's "Look for it when" cues and find one this notice breaks.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 15's questions in your casefile, starting on page 23. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “Ran away from the Subscriber's home on Sapponic, in Prince George County — 14 or 15 Weeks ago, a Mulatto Man Slave, named Tom, 25 Years old, about 5 feet 8 or 9 Inches high, thin faced, and bushy hair, if not cut off; he is very likely to grin when he speaks, or is spoken to; had on an old dark thick twilled coat, with plain yellow metal buttons; Has been several times captured, and escaped again before he could be delivered to the master whom unto he belonged; and the last time shackled, handcuffed, and an iron collar about his neck, with prongs… Whoever will deliver him to me, in Charles-City County, shall have a Reward of gold coins, besides what the law allows… by John Stith. Note: It is suspected he will seek to escape on Board some Vessel.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Ran away from my home on Sapponic, in Prince George County, 14 or 15 weeks ago: a Mulatto (mixed-race) Man Slave, named Tom, 25 years old. He is about 5 feet 8 or 9 inches tall, with a thin face and bushy hair, if it has not been cut off. He is very likely to grin when he speaks or is spoken to. He had on an old, dark, thick coat with plain yellow metal buttons. He has been several times captured, and escaped again before he could be returned to his master. The last time he was shackled, handcuffed, and had an iron collar about his neck, with prongs. Whoever brings him to me, in Charles City County, will get a reward of gold coins, plus what the law allows. By John Stith. Note: He may try to escape on board some ship.”

docs.title: Join, or Die
docs.src: Source: political cartoon, Pennsylvania Gazette, 9 May 1754. Attributed to Benjamin Franklin.

steps.question: Who made this, where did it appear, and why does that matter?
steps.line: Read the source line: who printed it, where, and on what day. Then ask what a printer wants when he runs a picture beside his own article.

Look first, before you read anything else: count the pieces and read the letters on each. One thing Franklin's readers knew: a popular belief said a snake cut into pieces before sundown would join back together and come alive.

steps.question: What is the picture arguing?
steps.line: Put the snake belief together with the two words at the bottom. What happens to the pieces if they stay apart?

steps.question: Who is in the snake, and who is left out?
steps.line: Match each set of letters to a colony. Count them. Then count the thirteen colonies you know.

steps.question: Why would separate colonies joining together matter to their safety and their freedom?
steps.line: Think back to Miantonomo in Document 4. Then look in the group called How power is built and limited.

docs.title: The article it ran with
docs.src: Franklin in the Pennsylvania Gazette, 9 May 1754

steps.question: Who wrote this, where was it printed, and what did he want readers to do?
steps.line: The heading names the writer and the paper. Look back at Document 16: it ran on the same page, on the same day.
Two parts: first the news from the Ohio Valley, then Franklin's opinion. Read the numbers carefully. A purse here means a treasury, a shared supply of money.

steps.question: What does Franklin say the colonies' problem is?
steps.line: Find the words "disunited State." Then find what he says the French have that the colonies don't.

steps.question: Is this news, an argument, or both? How might a colonist who didn't want to unite read it?
steps.line: Look at the order: the numbers first, then the blame. Ask what that order does to a reader.

steps.question: What would the colonies have to give up to become "one Council"?
steps.line: Ask who would make the decisions if the colonies joined. Then look in the group called How power is built and limited.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 16b's questions in your casefile, starting on page 27. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “Friday last an Express message arrived here from Major Washington, that Mr. Ward… was compelled to surrender his small fort in the Ohio River Valley to the French… the French had a Fleet of 360 Battleships and Canoes, upwards of 1000 Men, and 18 Pieces of Artillery… and Mr. Ward and the American colonists having but 44 Men, and no Cannon to make a proper Defense, was obliged to surrender…”

“…The Confidence of the French in this seems well-grounded on the present disunited State of the British Colonies, and the extreme Difficulty of bringing so many different Governments and Assemblies to agree in any speedy and effectual Measures for our common Defence and Security; while our Enemies have the very great Advantage of being under one Direction, with one Council, and one Purse.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Last Friday an urgent message arrived here from Major Washington. Mr. Ward was forced to surrender his small fort in the Ohio River Valley to the French. The French had a fleet of 360 battleships and canoes, more than 1000 men, and 18 cannons. Mr. Ward and the American colonists had only 44 men and no cannon to defend themselves, so they had to surrender.”

“The French feel confident because of the present disunited State of the British Colonies. It is very hard to get so many different governments and assemblies to agree quickly on a plan to defend us all. Meanwhile, our enemies have the very great advantage of being under one Direction, with one Council, and one Purse (one leader, one government, and one treasury).”

docs.title: Who gets to choose
docs.src: Source: Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, Section 1, January 14, 1639.

steps.question: Who wrote these rules, and who were they written for?
steps.line: Read the source line: 1639, Connecticut, and Section 1. The towns wrote these rules for themselves.
One very long sentence. Break it at each colon and semicolon. Magistrates are officials who run the government and act as judges.

steps.question: How is a governor chosen, and who gets to choose?
steps.line: Find the words "Court of Election." Then find "which choice shall be made by" near the end, and read everything after it.

steps.question: Who might be left out of "all that are admitted freemen"?
steps.line: Read the three things a voter had to be. Ask who in 1639 Connecticut could not meet all three.

steps.question: What principle does this document put into practice?
steps.line: Ask where the governor's power comes from in this document. Then look in the group called Where government's power comes from.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 17's questions in your casefile, starting on page 30. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: . . . It is Ordered, sentenced, and decreed, that there shall be yearly two General Assemblies or Courts, the one the second Thursday in April, the other the second Thursday in September following; the first shall be called the Court of Election, wherein shall be yearly chosen from time to time, so many Magistrates and other public Officers as shall be found requisite [needed]: Whereof one to be chosen Governor for the year ensuing and another be chosen, and no other Magistrate to be chosen for more than one year: provided always there be six chosen besides the Governor, which being chosen and sworn according to an Oath recorded for that purpose, shall have the power to administer justice according to the Laws here established, and for want thereof, according to the Rule of the Word of God; which choice shall be made by all that are admitted freemen and have taken the Oath of Fidelity, and do cohabit within this Jurisdiction having been admitted inhabitants by the major part of the Town wherein they live or the major part of such as shall be then present. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: It is ordered that there will be two General Assemblies or Courts every year, one on the second Thursday in April and the other on the second Thursday in September. The first one will be called the Court of Election. At it, every year, the people will choose as many Magistrates (officials and judges) and other public officers as are needed.

One of them will be chosen Governor for the coming year. No Magistrate will be chosen for more than one year at a time. There must always be six chosen besides the Governor. Once they are chosen and take their oath, they will have the power to give out justice according to the laws made here. Where there is no law, they will follow the Word of God.

The choice will be made by all who are admitted freemen, who have taken the Oath of Fidelity (loyalty), and who live in this area, after being accepted as residents by most of the people in their town.

docs.title: And who cannot
docs.src: Source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, Chapter 15, “Of Husband and Wife,” 1765.

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and why would a description of old law be hard to argue with?
steps.line: Read the Before you read note: nobody had to pass this. Ask what it takes to fight a rule no one remembers making.
Read the Before you read note first. Then two quotes, the first one long. Feme-covert and coverture are law-French; the easier version explains them.

steps.question: What happens to a woman's legal existence when she marries?
steps.line: Find the word "suspended." Read the words right before it and right after it.

steps.question: Whose account of the same marriage is missing from this page?
steps.line: Blackstone explains the rule from the law's side. Ask who lived under the rule and never got to write about it here.

steps.question: Put Documents 17 and 18 together. Who did self-government include in colonial America, and who did it leave out?
steps.line: Document 17 says who may choose. This one says who has no legal existence of her own. Then look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 18's questions in your casefile, starting on page 33. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “By marriage, the husband and wife are one person in law: that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least is incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband: under whose wing, protection, and cover, she performs everything; and is therefore called in our law-French a feme-covert… and her condition during her marriage is called her coverture.”
“Upon this principle, of an union of person in husband and wife, depend almost all the legal rights, duties, and disabilities, that either of them acquire by the marriage.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “When they marry, the husband and wife become one person in the eyes of the law. That means the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended (put on hold) during the marriage, or at least it is folded into her husband's. She does everything under his wing, protection, and cover. So in our law she is called a feme-covert (a covered woman), and her condition while married is called her coverture.”
“Almost all the legal rights, duties, and limits that a husband or wife gets from marriage come from this one rule: that the two of them are one person.”

note.title: Before you read
note.text: Before you read. The colonies ran on English common law, and this is the clearest statement of the rule that governed every married woman in them. It was written in 1765 — just after the period this unit covers — because it describes law already centuries old. Nobody had to pass this. It was simply how things were.

q4_card.title: Civic Principles
q4_card.intro: Q4 · CIVIC CONNECTION asks which principle is at stake. Name it from this card, then show how the document upholds it, denies it, or fights over it.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Rule of Law
items.question: No one is above the law, not even the people who make it. Look for it when someone powerful is held to the rules, or tries to dodge them.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Limited Government
items.question: Government can only do what the Constitution allows. Look for it when someone says the government went too far.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Separation of Powers
items.question: Power is split among three branches, each with its own job: make laws, carry out laws, judge laws. Look for it when the fight is about which branch gets to act.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Checks and Balances
items.question: Each branch can block or limit the others. Look for it when there's a veto, an override, an impeachment, or a court striking something down.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Federalism
items.question: Power is divided between the national government and the states. When they clash, valid federal law wins. Look for it when it's the nation against a state.

items.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED
items.name: Judicial Review
items.question: Courts can strike down a law or action that breaks the Constitution. Look for it when a court decides whether something is constitutional.

items.name: Popular Sovereignty (consent of the governed)
items.question: Government's power comes from the people, and it rules only with their agreement. Look for it when people give, or take back, their support for a government.

items.name: Representative Government
items.question: The people elect officials to make decisions for them. Look for it when the issue is voting, elections, or who speaks for whom.

items.name: Natural Rights
items.question: Every person is born with rights (life, liberty, property) that government exists to protect. Look for it when a right is treated as something you're born with, not something government hands out.

items.name: Individual Rights (civil liberties)
items.question: Freedoms government can't take away, like speech, religion, press and assembly. Look for it when a personal freedom is limited, defended, or expanded.

items.name: Equal Protection
items.question: The law must treat people equally. Look for it when a group is treated differently, shut out, or separated by law.

items.name: Due Process
items.question: Government must follow fair steps before it takes your life, liberty, or property. Look for it when someone is arrested, held, or punished. Ask whether it was fair.

close: Learn these by name. The Regents asks for them. Practice them in the Arena's matching set.
